I'm a registered nurse. I've spent over $6,000 of my own money trying to fix my acne scars in the last 4 years.
Almost every other woman I know with atrophic scars has done the same thing. Most of them have spent more.
I'm 36. I had cystic acne from 16 to 22. The acne cleared. The scars never did. Atrophic. Ice picks on both cheeks, rolling along my jaw.
I work in a clinic. I have professional access to the same treatments my patients pay full price for. I should have figured this out faster than I did.
I've done 2 rounds of fractional CO2.
3 rounds of in-clinic microneedling.
Chemical peels for over a year.
Tretinoin every night for almost a decade.
The Korean PDRN serums every brand started selling last year — 3 of them, around $80 each.
Last month, when my laser tech told me I needed "another 2 rounds at minimum" to see real change, I sat in my car and counted the bottles in my bathroom that didn't work.
I counted the receipts I've been keeping in a folder so my husband doesn't see them on the credit card statement.
And I drove home and cried in the bathroom for an hour.
Not because of the money.
Because I have a folder of who I used to be. Photos from 23, 24. Before. And I haven't looked at them in 3 years because the woman in those photos doesn't recognise the woman in the mirror anymore.
I cancel things now.
I cancelled brunch last weekend because the restaurant has overhead lighting.
I haven't taken a photo of myself in 2 years that wasn't filtered.
My husband loves me. He tells me the scars aren't a big deal. I know he means it.
But I see how I look in the front-facing camera in my bathroom and I think, this is the version of me he sees.
This is the version of me my daughter is going to remember.
That's what I'm actually paying $4,800 to make stop. Not the scars. The version of myself I've become because of them.
So when the laser tech said "another 2 rounds," I didn't say yes. I didn't say no.
I just smiled and said I'd think about it.
And then I went home and did what I should have done years ago. I read the actual literature.
Not Reddit, not blogs. PubMed. Dermatology journals. Molecular weight charts.
And what I found made me angry.
An atrophic scar isn't damage on the surface. It's a pit. A hole. Collapsed collagen, sitting more than a millimetre down in your dermis.
Laser doesn't fill that hole. Laser injures the surface and hopes the body rebuilds correctly on the way back up. Sometimes it works. Often it doesn't, and the patient comes back for round 2, round 3, round 4.
Microneedling at a clinic doesn't fill the hole either. The needles open channels, but if nothing's being delivered into them, the channels just close back up empty.
Topical serums physically cannot reach the layer where the scar lives. The PDRN molecule is between 50 and 1,500 kilodaltons.
Your skin barrier excludes anything above 500 daltons. The number isn't close. It's three orders of magnitude off.
Every Korean serum I'd bought, sitting half-empty on my bathroom counter, was never going to do anything.
Not because the ingredient was wrong. Because the delivery was wrong.
Every single treatment I'd tried was attacking the wrong layer.
$6,000 of treatments. All of them aimed at the wrong place.
I didn't fail at fixing my scars. I was sold an outdated model of how scars actually work, by an industry that profits from selling the next round.
The only thing in clinical practice that fills atrophic scars from the inside out is PDRN injected into the scar bed. Korean dermatologists do it. $600 a session. 3 sessions minimum.
I'd already spent $6,000. I wasn't paying another $1,800 to fly to Seoul.
The literature led me to a brand that built the at-home version. 24 gold-plated micro-needles, thinner than a hair. You press it on for 60 seconds. It opens 24 channels through the barrier the molecule can't cross alone. The PDRN flows down those channels into the layer where the scar actually is.
Same molecule. Same delivery principle as the clinic.
Twice a month. 5 minutes.
I almost didn't buy it.
I'd been burned $6,000 worth of times. One more $99 wasn't going to break me, but emotionally I was done.
I bought it anyway because of one thing the company said.
90 days, risk-free. If your scars don't shift, you send it back.
I started in March.
Week 1, nothing. Of course nothing.
Week 3, I noticed a photo I took with my daughter. The deep ones by my nose weren't catching the light the way they always do.
Week 6, I held eye contact with the woman behind the deli counter for a second longer than I normally would. I didn't realise I was doing it until I got to the car.
Week 10, I went to brunch. Outdoors. Overhead sun. I didn't think about it once until I was already home.
It's not a miracle. The deepest ice picks are still there. They're shallower. They don't grab the light the way they did. I stopped flinching at the front-facing camera.
I just took a photo of myself yesterday in the same bathroom I cried in 3 months ago.
It didn’t make me want to cry again.
It's called ELIXA. Same molecule the Korean clinics inject.
90 days, risk-free. If your scars don't shift, send it back.
I wish I'd found it before the $6,000. I wish someone with my background had told me 4 years ago what the molecular weight chart says.

Every single treatment I'd tried was attacking the wrong layer.
$6,000 of treatments. All of them aimed at the wrong place.
I didn't fail at fixing my scars. I was sold an outdated model of how scars actually work, by an industry that profits from selling the next round.
The only thing in clinical practice that fills atrophic scars from the inside out is PDRN injected into the scar bed. Korean dermatologists do it. $600 a session. 3 sessions minimum.
I'd already spent $6,000. I wasn't paying another $1,800 to fly to Seoul.
The literature led me to a brand that built the at-home version. 24 gold-plated micro-needles, thinner than a hair. You press it on for 60 seconds. It opens 24 channels through the barrier the molecule can't cross alone. The PDRN flows down those channels into the layer where the scar actually is.
Same molecule. Same delivery principle as the clinic.
Twice a month. 5 minutes.
I almost didn't buy it.
I'd been burned $6,000 worth of times. One more $99 wasn't going to break me, but emotionally I was done.
I bought it anyway because of one thing the company said.
90 days, risk-free. If your scars don't shift, you send it back.
I started in March.
Week 1, nothing. Of course nothing.
Week 3, I noticed a photo I took with my daughter. The deep ones by my nose weren't catching the light the way they always do.
Week 6, I held eye contact with the woman behind the deli counter for a second longer than I normally would. I didn't realise I was doing it until I got to the car.
Week 10, I went to brunch. Outdoors. Overhead sun. I didn't think about it once until I was already home.
It's not a miracle. The deepest ice picks are still there. They're shallower. They don't grab the light the way they did. I stopped flinching at the front-facing camera.
I just took a photo of myself yesterday in the same bathroom I cried in 3 months ago.
It didn’t make me want to cry again.
It's called ELIXA. Same molecule the Korean clinics inject.
90 days, risk-free. If your scars don't shift, send it back.
I wish I'd found it before the $6,000. I wish someone with my background had told me 4 years ago what the molecular weight chart says.

🚨 Must-Read Before Getting ‘Onda Lifting’ in Korea! (How to Boost Results by 200%)
Are you just lying there during your Onda Lifting? 🙅‍♀️ You might not see any results that way!
Remember these 3 things before you go to the clinic!
✅ POINT 1. Lift your chin all the way up!
The Onda tip (handpiece) is bigger than you think.
You need to lift your chin as high as possible for the energy to make perfect contact with your skin. Especially if you don’t have much double chin fat,
you need to lift high to definitely get the #Tightening and #FatDestruction effects you want! 🔥
✅ POINT 2. Turn your head side to side!
With Onda, the heat rises as the energy builds up.
If it stays in one spot, it can get too hot!
Show some sense by turning your head left and right (while keeping your chin up!)
to help the energy spread evenly over a wider area👀
✅ POINT 3. Wear a low-neckline top (Pro Tip 🍯)
We use ‘Jojoba Oil’ during the Onda procedure.
High-neck tops are inconvenient because you’ll have to get changed. If you come wearing a top that exposes your neckline, you can get the treatment comfortably right away without changing clothes or worrying about oil getting on them! 👚
Save this post and make sure to check it before your appointment! 💾

The auto-pay for the boat came out of my checking account on the 3rd of every month for the last 34 months.
Three hundred and forty dollars.
For 34 months.
That's $11,560 for a boat that's been sitting under a blue tarp in our side yard, next to the propane tank, growing a small colony of wasps under the bow.
My husband Bernard doesn't know I've been paying it.
He thinks we let it go two years ago. He thinks the finance company took it back. He thinks the tarp is covering a chest freezer.
It's not. It's covering a 19-foot Lund Impact XS that we picked out together on his second-to-last day at UPPCO before he retired.
I've been paying that boat payment out of the tips I make at the salon. Twenty-dollar tips. Sometimes a folded fifty at Christmas. I put them in an envelope in my glovebox and once a month I deposit the envelope at the credit union drive-through and pray my auto-pay clears.
I couldn't tell you why I've been doing this except that the day we bought that boat was the last day I saw my husband happy.
And I wasn't ready to let that day be the last one.
My name is Colleen. I'm 62 years old. I've been cutting hair in Escanaba, Michigan for 38 years, and I work three chairs down from where I started, at a salon on Ludington Street called Cutting Edge that's had the same green awning since 1994.
My husband Bernard is 63. He retired three years ago in August from Upper Peninsula Power Company after 38 years on the poles. He climbed them in blizzards. He climbed them in ice storms. He climbed them in July when the black flies were biting through his coveralls. He came home more than once with frostbite on his cheekbones.
For 38 years he did that job. And when I say his knees were shot, I mean shot in a way you can't fix with ice and Tylenol.
The retirement plan was the boat.
We are Yoopers. In Escanaba, if you don't fish, I don't know what you do. Bernard grew up fishing Little Bay de Noc with his dad and his uncle Wayne. When his dad passed in 2013, Bernard fished with just Wayne. When Wayne passed in 2019, Bernard fished alone.
The plan was that once he retired he'd fish every day the weather let him. He'd take the boat out on the bay at 5:30 in the morning. He'd bring home walleye and I'd cook them in butter with sliced almonds the way my mother taught me. We'd have the grandkids up in the summer and Bernard would take them out and teach them what his dad taught him.
That was the plan.
Here's what actually happened.
The week Bernard retired, he tried to climb into the boat at the launch off M-35 and his right knee buckled so hard he had to sit down on the trailer fender for 20 minutes before he could stand up again. He got in eventually. He caught 6 walleye that day. He came home smiling.
But it took him an hour and 12 minutes to get out of the boat when he came back to the launch.
I know because he told me. He didn't call for help. He didn't want another fisherman to see him. He sat in the boat at his own trailer and waited until the parking lot cleared out, and then he pulled himself up by the console and stepped over the gunwale one leg at a time like he was climbing over a fence in slow motion.
He drove home. He unhooked the trailer. He put the boat in the side yard. And he came in and sat down in his chair and didn't say anything for the whole night.
He went out 3 more times that first summer. Each one was worse than the last. By September he'd stopped talking about the bay.
The doctor said knee replacement. Both knees. Bernard said not yet.
I understand why he said not yet. His brother Ronnie got a knee replacement in 2016 and had a blood clot that put him in the hospital in Marquette for 11 days. Bernard watched Ronnie limp for a year afterward and said, "I'll live with what I got."
So we lived with it.
He tried a glucosamine chondroitin from Meijer. Nothing.
He tried turmeric. Nothing.
He tried a copper knee sleeve his cousin recommended. Nothing.
He tried CBD gummies my daughter mailed him from Traverse City. He said they made him sleepy but the knees still hurt.
He got a cortisone shot in October of that first year. It helped for about 5 weeks. He got another one 4 months later and it didn't do much of anything. The orthopedic in Marquette said he couldn't keep doing them forever.
So Bernard stopped trying.
That's the part I want you to understand. He didn't just have bad knees. He stopped trying.
A man who climbed a 40-foot pole in a snowstorm at 3:47 in the morning to get power back to St. Francis Hospital in 1994 stopped trying to walk down to the mailbox.
He sat in his chair. He watched hunting shows. He watched fishing shows, which is worse. He'd watch a man on the Fox Sports channel catching walleye on Mille Lacs and he'd get this look on his face like somebody was reading his will out loud.
I'd come home from the salon at 6 in the evening and find him in the exact same position I left him in at 8:30 in the morning. Same coffee cup. Same throw blanket. Same view of the same corner of the same room.
The tarp in the side yard was slowly caving in from the snow.
I couldn't call the finance company.
I don't know how to explain it any better than that. I just couldn't do it. Signing the paperwork to let that boat go felt like signing something else, and I couldn't put my name on it.
So I started using the tips.
The turning point came in June.
Bernard's cousin Kirby has a fish camp on Little Bay de Noc, about 40 minutes north on County Road 513. Every year for as long as I've known Bernard, the men in his family have gone up there for a long weekend in June. His dad went. His uncle Wayne went. His brother Ronnie went. Bernard went every single year from age 14 until age 60.
Kirby called on a Wednesday night. Bernard put him on speaker.
"You coming up this year, Bernie?"
Bernard was quiet for a second.
Then he said, "I don't think so this year, Kirb."
Kirby said, "You said that last year."
Bernard said, "I know."
Kirby said, "You gonna come next year?"
And Bernard didn't answer.
He just sat there in his chair, and Kirby waited on the line, and I stood in the kitchen with a wooden spoon in my hand and a pot of chicken and dumplings I'd stopped stirring, and eventually Kirby said, "Alright, Bern. I love ya. Call me if it changes."
Bernard hung up the phone and put his hand over his eyes.
He didn't cry. Bernard doesn't cry. His father didn't cry when his mother died. His grandfather didn't cry when his brother died in Korea. Bernards don't cry.
But he put his hand over his eyes for a long time.
And I stood in the kitchen and I knew he was giving up.
I knew it the way you know a customer has been drinking before she sits in your chair, or the way you know a marriage is over before either spouse says the word. You know because you've been paying attention.
I stirred the dumplings.
And I thought about the tarp in the side yard and the $340 leaving my checking account on the 3rd of the next month, and I felt something in me get very quiet.
I had two choices. I could stop paying the boat and let it go, and Bernard could sit in that chair until he couldn't get out of it, and one day I'd bury him and drive past Kirby's camp on 513 and cry.
Or I could figure something out.
I don't know why I thought I could figure something out. I'm a hairdresser. I don't have any credentials. I don't have any special knowledge. I cut and colored hair for 38 years and raised two kids and made pasties every Christmas Eve.
But I had a chair every day. And people talk in that chair.
Eileen has been my Tuesday-morning 9:15 for 14 years. She's 67. She gets a wash and set every other Tuesday and a permanent wave every 4 months. Her husband Sigurd is a retired welder from the shipyard down in Marinette. Sig is 71 and until 2 years ago he could barely get out of a kitchen chair.
I didn't know this until Eileen sat down that particular Tuesday, two weeks after Kirby's phone call, and asked how Bernard was doing.
I looked at her in the mirror.
And instead of saying "good" the way I usually do, I said, "He's not doing good, Eileen. He hasn't been in that boat in almost two years."
Eileen was quiet while I combed her out.
Then she said, "Sig couldn't get up off the couch in 2022. You remember that?"
I remembered. Sig had missed the Delta County Fair for the first time in his adult life. Eileen had come in for her permanent wave the week after and cried into her cape.
"He's back at the shop now," she said. "Three days a week. He rebuilt the transmission on our grandson's Ranger last month."
I stopped combing.
"How?"
Eileen said, "My sister-in-law Maureen sent him something."
I want to be careful here about how I tell this part, because I don't want you to think Eileen sold me on anything. She didn't. She was talking about her husband. I was the one asking questions.
Eileen said Maureen's daughter is a nurse in a rehabilitation clinic outside of Green Bay. And Maureen's daughter had a patient, an older gentleman, who came in after a hip surgery and was recovering way faster than anybody expected. He told Maureen's daughter he'd been taking something for a couple of months before the surgery. Something with a fruit called amla.
Maureen's daughter looked it up.
She told Maureen. Maureen told Eileen. Eileen ordered a bottle for Sig.
Two months later Sig was up.
I finished Eileen's permanent that morning and I did not think about it for the rest of my shift because I had 4 clients back to back and a bride's rehearsal party at 4 in the afternoon.
But when I got home that night, I sat in my car in the driveway with my phone and I typed in a-m-l-a and I read for about 40 minutes with the engine off and the windows fogging up.
Here is what I understood by the time I went inside.
The problem in Bernard's knees wasn't just wear and tear. That's what I'd been told for years. That's what the orthopedic said. That's what every article in the AARP magazine said. Wear and tear.
But wear and tear is a description. It's not a cause.
The actual cause, or one of them anyway, is that the cells inside our joints need energy to maintain themselves. To keep the cartilage smooth. To keep the fluid where it belongs. To manage the low-level inflammation that happens every day in every joint of every human alive.
That energy is made by tiny structures inside every cell called mitochondria. You may have heard of them from a middle-school science class. The powerhouse of the cell. That's what they called them in 1978 when I was in Mrs. Aikens's class.
Well. As we age, and as we spend 38 years climbing power poles in the freezing cold, our mitochondria don't work the way they used to. They lose efficiency. They put out less energy.
And when the cells in your joints aren't getting the energy they need, they can't do their maintenance work. Cartilage doesn't stay smooth. The joint environment gets inflamed. Everything hurts.
I read this and I thought about Bernard's chair.
I thought about the glucosamine that didn't work. And the turmeric that didn't work. And the copper sleeves and the CBD and the cortisone.
Something Maureen's daughter had explained to Eileen finally landed for me. She'd said it was like sending a construction crew to a job site with all their lumber and nails and tools but no electricity. They can't run the saw. They can't run the drill. They can't do the work. It doesn't matter how much lumber you send.
Bernard's joints had been getting lumber for years. Glucosamine. Turmeric. Copper. They just didn't have any power to do anything with it.
Amla, from what I read, is different because of what it does to a pathway called AMPK.
I'm not a scientist. I'm going to explain this the way I understood it sitting in my Buick.
AMPK is like a switch inside your cells. When it's on, the cells make more energy and manage themselves better. When it's off, or working poorly, they don't. Amla is one of the few things that seems to reliably turn that switch on. It supports your mitochondria at the source instead of just throwing more raw material at cells that can't use it.
The active compounds in amla are called emblicanins. They're antioxidants but they also do something antioxidants don't usually do. They seem to signal to the cell to work better.
That was the piece I hadn't heard before.
Every supplement Bernard had tried was trying to add something to his joints. Amla was trying to help the cells in his joints do their own job again.
I went inside. Bernard was in his chair. I made grilled cheese and tomato soup and we watched half of a fishing show and he fell asleep before it ended.

The auto-pay for the boat came out of my checking account on the 3rd of every month for the last 34 months.
Three hundred and forty dollars.
For 34 months.
That's $11,560 for a boat that's been sitting under a blue tarp in our side yard, next to the propane tank, growing a small colony of wasps under the bow.
My husband Bernard doesn't know I've been paying it.
He thinks we let it go two years ago. He thinks the finance company took it back. He thinks the tarp is covering a chest freezer.
It's not. It's covering a 19-foot Lund Impact XS that we picked out together on his second-to-last day at UPPCO before he retired.
I've been paying that boat payment out of the tips I make at the salon. Twenty-dollar tips. Sometimes a folded fifty at Christmas. I put them in an envelope in my glovebox and once a month I deposit the envelope at the credit union drive-through and pray my auto-pay clears.
I couldn't tell you why I've been doing this except that the day we bought that boat was the last day I saw my husband happy.
And I wasn't ready to let that day be the last one.
My name is Colleen. I'm 62 years old. I've been cutting hair in Escanaba, Michigan for 38 years, and I work three chairs down from where I started, at a salon on Ludington Street called Cutting Edge that's had the same green awning since 1994.
My husband Bernard is 63. He retired three years ago in August from Upper Peninsula Power Company after 38 years on the poles. He climbed them in blizzards. He climbed them in ice storms. He climbed them in July when the black flies were biting through his coveralls. He came home more than once with frostbite on his cheekbones.
For 38 years he did that job. And when I say his knees were shot, I mean shot in a way you can't fix with ice and Tylenol.
The retirement plan was the boat.
We are Yoopers. In Escanaba, if you don't fish, I don't know what you do. Bernard grew up fishing Little Bay de Noc with his dad and his uncle Wayne. When his dad passed in 2013, Bernard fished with just Wayne. When Wayne passed in 2019, Bernard fished alone.
The plan was that once he retired he'd fish every day the weather let him. He'd take the boat out on the bay at 5:30 in the morning. He'd bring home walleye and I'd cook them in butter with sliced almonds the way my mother taught me. We'd have the grandkids up in the summer and Bernard would take them out and teach them what his dad taught him.
That was the plan.
Here's what actually happened.
The week Bernard retired, he tried to climb into the boat at the launch off M-35 and his right knee buckled so hard he had to sit down on the trailer fender for 20 minutes before he could stand up again. He got in eventually. He caught 6 walleye that day. He came home smiling.
But it took him an hour and 12 minutes to get out of the boat when he came back to the launch.
I know because he told me. He didn't call for help. He didn't want another fisherman to see him. He sat in the boat at his own trailer and waited until the parking lot cleared out, and then he pulled himself up by the console and stepped over the gunwale one leg at a time like he was climbing over a fence in slow motion.
He drove home. He unhooked the trailer. He put the boat in the side yard. And he came in and sat down in his chair and didn't say anything for the whole night.
He went out 3 more times that first summer. Each one was worse than the last. By September he'd stopped talking about the bay.
The doctor said knee replacement. Both knees. Bernard said not yet.
I understand why he said not yet. His brother Ronnie got a knee replacement in 2016 and had a blood clot that put him in the hospital in Marquette for 11 days. Bernard watched Ronnie limp for a year afterward and said, "I'll live with what I got."
So we lived with it.
He tried a glucosamine chondroitin from Meijer. Nothing.
He tried turmeric. Nothing.
He tried a copper knee sleeve his cousin recommended. Nothing.
He tried CBD gummies my daughter mailed him from Traverse City. He said they made him sleepy but the knees still hurt.
He got a cortisone shot in October of that first year. It helped for about 5 weeks. He got another one 4 months later and it didn't do much of anything. The orthopedic in Marquette said he couldn't keep doing them forever.
So Bernard stopped trying.
That's the part I want you to understand. He didn't just have bad knees. He stopped trying.
A man who climbed a 40-foot pole in a snowstorm at 3:47 in the morning to get power back to St. Francis Hospital in 1994 stopped trying to walk down to the mailbox.
He sat in his chair. He watched hunting shows. He watched fishing shows, which is worse. He'd watch a man on the Fox Sports channel catching walleye on Mille Lacs and he'd get this look on his face like somebody was reading his will out loud.
I'd come home from the salon at 6 in the evening and find him in the exact same position I left him in at 8:30 in the morning. Same coffee cup. Same throw blanket. Same view of the same corner of the same room.
The tarp in the side yard was slowly caving in from the snow.
I couldn't call the finance company.
I don't know how to explain it any better than that. I just couldn't do it. Signing the paperwork to let that boat go felt like signing something else, and I couldn't put my name on it.
So I started using the tips.
The turning point came in June.
Bernard's cousin Kirby has a fish camp on Little Bay de Noc, about 40 minutes north on County Road 513. Every year for as long as I've known Bernard, the men in his family have gone up there for a long weekend in June. His dad went. His uncle Wayne went. His brother Ronnie went. Bernard went every single year from age 14 until age 60.
Kirby called on a Wednesday night. Bernard put him on speaker.
"You coming up this year, Bernie?"
Bernard was quiet for a second.
Then he said, "I don't think so this year, Kirb."
Kirby said, "You said that last year."
Bernard said, "I know."
Kirby said, "You gonna come next year?"
And Bernard didn't answer.
He just sat there in his chair, and Kirby waited on the line, and I stood in the kitchen with a wooden spoon in my hand and a pot of chicken and dumplings I'd stopped stirring, and eventually Kirby said, "Alright, Bern. I love ya. Call me if it changes."
Bernard hung up the phone and put his hand over his eyes.
He didn't cry. Bernard doesn't cry. His father didn't cry when his mother died. His grandfather didn't cry when his brother died in Korea. Bernards don't cry.
But he put his hand over his eyes for a long time.
And I stood in the kitchen and I knew he was giving up.
I knew it the way you know a customer has been drinking before she sits in your chair, or the way you know a marriage is over before either spouse says the word. You know because you've been paying attention.
I stirred the dumplings.
And I thought about the tarp in the side yard and the $340 leaving my checking account on the 3rd of the next month, and I felt something in me get very quiet.
I had two choices. I could stop paying the boat and let it go, and Bernard could sit in that chair until he couldn't get out of it, and one day I'd bury him and drive past Kirby's camp on 513 and cry.
Or I could figure something out.
I don't know why I thought I could figure something out. I'm a hairdresser. I don't have any credentials. I don't have any special knowledge. I cut and colored hair for 38 years and raised two kids and made pasties every Christmas Eve.
But I had a chair every day. And people talk in that chair.
Eileen has been my Tuesday-morning 9:15 for 14 years. She's 67. She gets a wash and set every other Tuesday and a permanent wave every 4 months. Her husband Sigurd is a retired welder from the shipyard down in Marinette. Sig is 71 and until 2 years ago he could barely get out of a kitchen chair.
I didn't know this until Eileen sat down that particular Tuesday, two weeks after Kirby's phone call, and asked how Bernard was doing.
I looked at her in the mirror.
And instead of saying "good" the way I usually do, I said, "He's not doing good, Eileen. He hasn't been in that boat in almost two years."
Eileen was quiet while I combed her out.
Then she said, "Sig couldn't get up off the couch in 2022. You remember that?"
I remembered. Sig had missed the Delta County Fair for the first time in his adult life. Eileen had come in for her permanent wave the week after and cried into her cape.
"He's back at the shop now," she said. "Three days a week. He rebuilt the transmission on our grandson's Ranger last month."
I stopped combing.
"How?"
Eileen said, "My sister-in-law Maureen sent him something."
I want to be careful here about how I tell this part, because I don't want you to think Eileen sold me on anything. She didn't. She was talking about her husband. I was the one asking questions.
Eileen said Maureen's daughter is a nurse in a rehabilitation clinic outside of Green Bay. And Maureen's daughter had a patient, an older gentleman, who came in after a hip surgery and was recovering way faster than anybody expected. He told Maureen's daughter he'd been taking something for a couple of months before the surgery. Something with a fruit called amla.
Maureen's daughter looked it up.
She told Maureen. Maureen told Eileen. Eileen ordered a bottle for Sig.
Two months later Sig was up.
I finished Eileen's permanent that morning and I did not think about it for the rest of my shift because I had 4 clients back to back and a bride's rehearsal party at 4 in the afternoon.
But when I got home that night, I sat in my car in the driveway with my phone and I typed in a-m-l-a and I read for about 40 minutes with the engine off and the windows fogging up.
Here is what I understood by the time I went inside.
The problem in Bernard's knees wasn't just wear and tear. That's what I'd been told for years. That's what the orthopedic said. That's what every article in the AARP magazine said. Wear and tear.
But wear and tear is a description. It's not a cause.
The actual cause, or one of them anyway, is that the cells inside our joints need energy to maintain themselves. To keep the cartilage smooth. To keep the fluid where it belongs. To manage the low-level inflammation that happens every day in every joint of every human alive.
That energy is made by tiny structures inside every cell called mitochondria. You may have heard of them from a middle-school science class. The powerhouse of the cell. That's what they called them in 1978 when I was in Mrs. Aikens's class.
Well. As we age, and as we spend 38 years climbing power poles in the freezing cold, our mitochondria don't work the way they used to. They lose efficiency. They put out less energy.
And when the cells in your joints aren't getting the energy they need, they can't do their maintenance work. Cartilage doesn't stay smooth. The joint environment gets inflamed. Everything hurts.
I read this and I thought about Bernard's chair.
I thought about the glucosamine that didn't work. And the turmeric that didn't work. And the copper sleeves and the CBD and the cortisone.
Something Maureen's daughter had explained to Eileen finally landed for me. She'd said it was like sending a construction crew to a job site with all their lumber and nails and tools but no electricity. They can't run the saw. They can't run the drill. They can't do the work. It doesn't matter how much lumber you send.
Bernard's joints had been getting lumber for years. Glucosamine. Turmeric. Copper. They just didn't have any power to do anything with it.
Amla, from what I read, is different because of what it does to a pathway called AMPK.
I'm not a scientist. I'm going to explain this the way I understood it sitting in my Buick.
AMPK is like a switch inside your cells. When it's on, the cells make more energy and manage themselves better. When it's off, or working poorly, they don't. Amla is one of the few things that seems to reliably turn that switch on. It supports your mitochondria at the source instead of just throwing more raw material at cells that can't use it.
The active compounds in amla are called emblicanins. They're antioxidants but they also do something antioxidants don't usually do. They seem to signal to the cell to work better.
That was the piece I hadn't heard before.
Every supplement Bernard had tried was trying to add something to his joints. Amla was trying to help the cells in his joints do their own job again.
I went inside. Bernard was in his chair. I made grilled cheese and tomato soup and we watched half of a fishing show and he fell asleep before it ended.
The next morning before work I went to the website Eileen had told me. Auniva. I ordered two bottles.
The website is [auniva.co/amla/33](https://l.facebook.com/l.php?u=http%3A%2F%2Fauniva.co%2Famla%2F33&h=AUCM0EQbplw_M1C3LNm0-O_vquowLUQi4mEQmlYkhtZVr6Ko3QRlo0qeXOKrRnyTOvuTiUZIqqHHHJJzq6azuP3DxnuH0ZyXwTguEgLEx8bU-ScvGyzXt9ybTanw8YE5f2-77Tg8eMo9NQrgr5AgP8gPQTT17Q)
I paid $34 dollars for the first bottle and got the second one at a discount. Shipping was free.
The bottles arrived in 5 days. Two capsules a day. 30 servings per bottle.
I put the first bottle on the counter next to Bernard's coffee cup on a Wednesday morning and he looked at it and said, "What's this?"
I said, "It's amla. Eileen's Sig has been taking it."
He said, "Sig can't walk."
I said, "Sig fixed a transmission last month."
Bernard looked at me for a long time.
And then he opened the bottle and took two capsules with his coffee.
Nothing happened for about 12 days.
I want to be honest about that because I know how these stories can sound. Bernard took his amla every morning with his coffee and for a week and a half nothing changed. He sat in the same chair. He watched the same shows. I paid the boat payment on the 3rd out of an envelope of tips.
Around day 15 I noticed him standing in the kitchen at the counter, not sitting at the table. Standing while he ate a bowl of cereal.
I didn't say anything.
At the end of week 3 I came home and he was outside. In the driveway. Just standing there looking at the tarp on the boat.
I didn't say anything about that either.
Week 4 he took the tarp off. It took him about 20 minutes because the wasps had built a nest under one corner. I watched from the kitchen window. He got a can of spray from the garage. He sprayed. He waited. He rolled the tarp back the rest of the way.
He walked around the boat once. Slowly.
He came back inside and had a beer.
Week 6 he called his cousin Kirby.
I was at the salon when he called. He told me later that night. He told Kirby he wasn't coming up to camp this June but that he might come up in September for the fall run. He said Kirby got quiet on the line the way Kirby does when something matters to him, and then Kirby said, "Alright, Bern. I'll hold a spot."
Week 8 he asked me for the keys to the truck.
He drove himself down to the launch off M-35. Alone. He didn't take the boat. He just drove down there and sat in the truck at the launch and watched other men back their trailers into the water for about an hour, and then he came home.
He didn't tell me he'd gone until I noticed the receipt from the gas station in Gladstone on the counter.
Week 11 he hooked up the trailer.
I was making eggs when he came in the kitchen and said, "I'm gonna take her out."
I said, "Today?"
He said, "Yeah."
I said, "Do you want me to come?"
He said, "No. I want to do it by myself first."
I said okay. I gave him a thermos of coffee and a peanut butter sandwich in a Ziploc.
He was gone from 6 in the morning until 2 in the afternoon.
He came back with 3 walleye and a small pike he threw back and skin that was pink from the sun for the first time in almost 3 years.
He backed the trailer into the driveway. He stepped out of the boat by himself, one leg at a time. It wasn't fast. It wasn't graceful. His knees are still his knees.
But he did it.
And he stood in the side yard with his hand on the gunwale for a minute, and he looked at the boat, and he looked at me on the back porch, and he said, "The auto-pay never went through on this thing, did it."
I sat down on the porch step.
I said, "It went through, Bern."
He said, "For how long?"
I said, "Since we stopped talking about it."
He came up the steps. He sat down next to me. He didn't say anything for a long time. And then he put his hand over his eyes the same way he did after the phone call with Kirby, and this time he did cry.
Just a little. Bernards don't cry a lot.
I want to tell you something about Auniva's Amla and the reason I'm sitting here typing this on my laptop at the kitchen table on a Sunday morning while Bernard's out on the bay.
I'm not a spokesperson. I cut hair. I'm 62 years old and I have arthritis in my thumbs from 38 years of holding shears and I probably need to think about what I'm going to take for that too.
But I'm sharing this because there are wives all over Delta County, and all over the Upper Peninsula, and all over this country, who are watching their husbands sit in chairs and give up on the things they used to love.
You've been told it's aging. You've been told there's nothing to do. You've been told the only real option is a surgery your husband won't agree to.
And in the meantime you've been paying for a boat, or a bass tracker, or a hunting camp, or a set of golf clubs, or a Harley in the garage, out of your tips or your Social Security or the sale of your mother's earrings, because you're not ready to let the last version of your husband disappear.
I understand you.
Auniva's Amla comes in a bottle of 60 capsules. 30 servings. Two capsules a day with breakfast or coffee. It's made in the USA. Shipping is free. And there's a 90-day money-back guarantee, which is what let me try it in the first place. If it hadn't worked for Bernard, I could have sent it back and gotten every dollar of my tip money back into that envelope.
You can go check it out at:

P.S. Bernard is going up to Kirby's camp on Little Bay de Noc in September for the fall run. He's the first one who called Kirby to confirm this year, ahead of Ronnie and ahead of Ronnie's son. Kirby told me on the phone last week that he almost dropped his coffee cup when Bernard's name came up on the caller ID. He said, "Coll, I didn't think he was ever gonna come back up here." Neither did I. That call is worth every $340 that came out of my checking account for 34 months, and I would pay it all over again for the sound of Bernard telling his cousin what tackle he wants to bring.
P.P.S. Auniva's 90-day money-back guarantee is the reason I want to say something specific. I've been on the wrong side of a lot of medical bills in this family. Bernard's cortisone shots were $180 each after insurance. The MRI he got in 2022 for his right knee was $1,240 out of pocket, and I never once saw a refund offered when the shots wore off, when the MRI showed nothing new, when the specialist charged us $340 for a visit that ended with "we'll just keep an eye on it." Nobody in medicine offers you your money back when they don't help you. Auniva does. If it doesn't work for your husband, or for you, you send back the bottles and you get every penny. That's a kind of confidence I've never seen from any of the specialists we've paid.
P.P.P.S. I need to mention something practical. Eileen told me a couple of months ago that when she went to reorder Sig's bottles, they were out of stock for about 10 days. This is a small company and they don't always keep pace with how many people are finding out about them. I keep 2 bottles at the house at all times now, one open and one sealed on the shelf, because I don't want Bernard to miss a day. I don't know what their inventory looks like this week. If your husband's fishing opener is in the spring, or if you've got a milestone coming up like a wedding or a grandchild's baptism or a family reunion where you'd like him to actually be present, I wouldn't wait. Bernard sat in that chair for two summers. He can't get those two summers back. I don't want that for you.

U40, là mẹ của 4 người con và hiện đang sinh sống tại Anh, chị tìm đến Bác sĩ Ngô Kiều Khanh với một mong muốn rất rõ ràng: cải thiện những dấu hiệu lão hóa nhưng vẫn giữ được nét tự nhiên của gương mặt.
Với mỗi khách hàng, Bác sĩ Khanh không lựa chọn công nghệ chỉ dựa trên độ “hot” của thiết bị.
Điều quan trọng hơn là tình trạng da, độ săn chắc của mô mềm, đường nét gương mặt và mục tiêu thẩm mỹ thực tế của từng người.
Sau khi trực tiếp thăm khám và đánh giá, Thermage FLX được lựa chọn trong kế hoạch trẻ hóa dành riêng cho chị.
𝐕𝐀̣̂𝐘 𝐕𝐈̀ 𝐒𝐀𝐎 𝐋𝐀̣𝐈 𝐋𝐀̀ 𝐓𝐇𝐄𝐑𝐌𝐀𝐆𝐄 𝐅𝐋𝐗?
Thermage FLX sử dụng công nghệ RF đơn cực (Monopolar Radiofrequency), đưa năng lượng nhiệt có kiểm soát vào mô, hỗ trợ quá trình co rút collagen và tái cấu trúc collagen theo thời gian.
Với một làn da U40 bắt đầu xuất hiện tình trạng kém săn chắc, đường nét gương mặt không còn rõ như trước và các dấu hiệu lão hóa ngày càng dễ nhận thấy, mục tiêu của liệu trình không nhất thiết phải là thay đổi thật nhiều.
Mà là hỗ trợ làn da săn chắc hơn, cải thiện độ rõ của đường nét và duy trì vẻ tự nhiên vốn có.
𝐌𝐄̣ 𝟒 𝐂𝐎𝐍 – 𝐊𝐇𝐎̂𝐍𝐆 𝐂𝐎́ 𝐍𝐆𝐇𝐈̃𝐀 𝐋𝐀̀ 𝐏𝐇𝐀̉𝐈 𝐓𝐇𝐀𝐘 Đ𝐎̂̉𝐈 𝐆𝐔̛𝐎̛𝐍𝐆 𝐌𝐀̣̆𝐓
Sau 4 lần mang thai và sinh con, cơ thể cũng như chất lượng mô mềm có thể trải qua nhiều thay đổi theo thời gian.
Vì vậy, thay vì áp dụng một công thức trẻ hóa giống nhau cho tất cả khách hàng, Bác sĩ Khanh tập trung vào việc đánh giá thực tế từng gương mặt để lựa chọn công nghệ và chiến lược phù hợp.
Với chị, điều cần hướng đến không phải một diện mạo “khác đi”.
Mà là một phiên bản săn chắc hơn, tươi trẻ hơn nhưng vẫn là chính mình.
🌿 Và có lẽ đây cũng là điều thú vị nhất của trẻ hóa ở tuổi U40.
Không phải cố gắng quay trở lại tuổi 20.
Mà là chăm sóc bản thân đúng lúc, để những dấu hiệu thời gian được kiểm soát tốt hơn và mình vẫn có thể tự tin với phiên bản hiện tại.
🏆 Tại phòng khám của Bác sĩ Ngô Kiều Khanh, mỗi liệu trình Thermage FLX đều bắt đầu từ bước đánh giá tình trạng da, mô mềm, cấu trúc gương mặt và mong muốn thẩm mỹ của từng khách hàng.
Không phải gương mặt nào cũng cần cùng một công nghệ. Và không phải cứ nhiều năng lượng hay nhiều lần thực hiện hơn thì sẽ tốt hơn.
Điều quan trọng là đúng tình trạng – đúng mục tiêu – đúng chiến lược.

𝐖𝐇𝐘 𝐃𝐈𝐃 𝐃𝐑. 𝐊𝐇𝐀𝐍𝐇 𝐂𝐇𝐎𝐎𝐒𝐄 𝐓𝐇𝐄𝐑𝐌𝐀𝐆𝐄 𝐅𝐋𝐗 𝐅𝐎𝐑 𝐀 𝐕𝐈𝐄𝐓𝐍𝐀𝐌𝐄𝐒𝐄 𝐖𝐎𝐌𝐀𝐍 𝐔𝐍𝐃𝐄𝐑 𝟒𝟎 – 𝐀 𝐌𝐎𝐓𝐇𝐄𝐑 𝐎𝐅 𝟒?
Under 40, a mother of four and currently living in the UK, she came to Dr. Ngô Kiều Khanh with a clear goal: to improve visible signs of aging while preserving the natural character of her face.
For every patient, Dr. Khanh does not choose a technology simply because it is “trending” or popular.
What matters more is the condition of the skin, the firmness of the soft tissue, facial contours, and each individual’s realistic aesthetic goals.
After a thorough in-person consultation and assessment, Thermage FLX was selected as part of a personalized rejuvenation plan designed specifically for her.
𝐒𝐎, 𝐖𝐇𝐘 𝐓𝐇𝐄𝐑𝐌𝐀𝐆𝐄 𝐅𝐋𝐗?
Thermage FLX uses Monopolar Radiofrequency (RF) technology to deliver controlled thermal energy into the tissue, supporting collagen contraction and collagen remodeling over time.
For U40 skin that is beginning to show reduced firmness, less-defined facial contours and increasingly visible signs of aging, the goal of treatment does not necessarily have to be dramatic transformation.
Instead, it is about supporting firmer-looking skin, enhancing facial definition and maintaining the natural appearance that is uniquely hers.
𝐁𝐄𝐈𝐍𝐆 𝐀 𝐌𝐎𝐓𝐇𝐄𝐑 𝐎𝐅 𝟒 𝐃𝐎𝐄𝐒 𝐍𝐎𝐓 𝐌𝐄𝐀𝐍 𝐘𝐎𝐔 𝐍𝐄𝐄𝐃 𝐀 𝐃𝐈𝐅𝐅𝐄𝐑𝐄𝐍𝐓 𝐅𝐀𝐂𝐄
After four pregnancies and childbirths, both the body and soft-tissue quality can naturally undergo various changes over time.
That is why, instead of applying the same rejuvenation formula to every patient, Dr. Khanh focuses on assessing each individual face and selecting the most appropriate technology and treatment strategy.
For her, the goal is not to create a completely “different” appearance.
It is to achieve a firmer, fresher and more youthful version of herself—while still looking like her.
🌿 And perhaps this is the most interesting part of rejuvenation in your 40s.
It is not about trying to go back to your 20s.
It is about taking care of yourself at the right time, so that the signs of time can be better managed while you continue to feel confident in the person you are today.
🏆 At Dr. Ngô Kiều Khanh’s clinic, every Thermage FLX treatment begins with an assessment of the patient’s skin condition, soft tissue, facial structure and individual aesthetic goals.
Not every face needs the same technology. And more energy or more treatment sessions do not necessarily mean better results.
What truly matters is the right condition – the right goal – the right strategy.
📩 If you are in your 30s or 40s and have started noticing reduced skin firmness, changes in facial contours, or simply want to take a proactive approach to skin aging before the signs become more pronounced, let Dr. Ngô Kiều Khanh personally assess your condition before choosing the most suitable technology.

ads.copy:
🇰🇷 韓國 SMILE Pro 只要台灣半價？揭密 10 秒雷射的真相！！！​大家最近是不是一直被 #韓國雷射 洗版？除了價格甜到不可思議，到底跟台灣的技術有什麼差別？今天幫大家整理了這份 #SMILEPro 終極懶人包，看完再決定要不要買機票！✈️
​🔍 為什麼選 SMILE Pro (VisuMax 800)？
簡單說，它是雷射界的法拉利，比起舊款 SMILE 有三大升級：
1️⃣ 超快速度 (Speed)： 單眼雷射時間從傳統的 25 秒縮短到 「8-10 秒」！根據臨床數據，這大幅降低了眼睛亂動導致失敗的風險。
2️⃣ 解決散光 (Astigmatism)： 這是最有感的升級！內建 OcuLign 智慧導航，如果你躺下時眼球旋轉，雷射會自動轉向追蹤。數據顯示，散光矯正的精準度因此大幅提升，不再只靠醫師憑感覺。
3️⃣ 恢復神速 (Recovery)： 傷口只有 2mm (筆尖大小)，保留了角膜強度。研究顯示 92% 的人術後 3 個月視力都在 1.0 以上。
​💰 價格大比拼 (台幣預估)
這也是大家最關心的！為什麼韓國這麼便宜？因為江南區的診所採用「工廠化」經營，量大成本低，且價格透明競爭。
🇹🇼 台灣： 約 8-14 萬 TWD
🇰🇷 韓國： 約 5-9.5 萬 TWD
👉 現省 3-4 萬！ 這筆錢拿來買機票、住飯店、吃醬蟹還有找！
​⚠️ 去韓國雷射的風險評估 (非常重要！必看！)
雖然 CP 值高，但醫療沒有 100% 的：
​術後回診難： 萬一回到台灣眼睛發炎，台灣醫師可能無法調閱韓國的手術數據，處理起來比較麻煩。
​術前停戴隱眼： 軟式至少 1 週，硬式 2-3 週。這點絕對不能偷懶，不然檢查數據不準，雷射打偏就慘了！
​隱形收費： 有些低價廣告不含藥水費或指定院長費，預約前要問清楚「Full Package Price」。
​💡 醫師怎麼看？
如果你是高度散光、容易緊張（怕痛、怕眼睛張不久）的人，SMILE Pro 的 10秒雷射 與 AI 輔助 絕對是首選。至於是留在台灣享受完整售後，還是飛韓國省錢，就看大家對風險的接受度囉！

My ex-husband invited me to his wedding. His new wife is 12 years younger than me. I went anyway. And by the end of the night, she was the one who looked rattled.
⠀
Eighteen years married. Two kids. A house with a garden I'd done myself. The same families on holiday with us every summer.
⠀
Then he left me for a 42-year-old called Gemma. I won't bore you with it. You know how these things go.
⠀
What you don't know is that eight months later, my two teenagers sat me down at the kitchen table and begged me to go to the wedding. "Mum, please. If you don't come it'll be awkward for everyone. People will think you're bitter." My daughter, who's 16, looked straight at me. "We need you there. We need people to see we're alright."
⠀
So I said yes. Not for him. Not for Gemma. For them.
⠀
I went down for their engagement party. Small restaurant. Candles everywhere. The sort of place that either flatters you or finishes you off, depending on where you're sat.
⠀
I looked dreadful. I knew it before I'd even gone in. The lines, and that grey, worn-out look to my skin, hadn't been this bad a year ago. But the divorce. The nights I didn't sleep. Starting again from nothing at 54. It had all settled on my face.
⠀
I sat near the back. Kept my head down. Smiled when I had to.
⠀
Then I nipped to the ladies'. And that's when I heard it. Two voices. One of them was Gemma's.
⠀
"I do feel a bit sorry for her," Gemma was saying. "She looks like she hasn't slept since the divorce. And her make-up, bless her." The bridesmaid laughed. Then Gemma said: "Someone should at least tell her to blend it in before the photos." More laughing.
⠀
I stood behind that cubicle door and didn't breathe.
⠀
She wasn't jealous of me. She didn't see me as any sort of threat. She felt sorry for me.
⠀
And honestly, that was worse than if she'd hated me. If someone hates you, you still matter. If they feel sorry for you, they've already written you off.
⠀
I got back to the hotel before I fell apart. Sat on the edge of the bath. Cried until my chest ached.
⠀
Then I got up. Went to the mirror. Hotel bathroom lighting. The cruellest light there is.
⠀
And I saw exactly what Gemma had seen. The heaviness. Foundation sitting on top of my skin like a mask. The spots. Brown patches coming through however much I put on. The crepiness. Thin, papery skin folding in on itself like tissue paper that's been screwed up. The fine lines round my eyes, every one of them filled with foundation.
⠀
I looked worn out. I looked old. I looked like a woman whose best years had been and gone.
⠀
And for about ten seconds, I believed it. Then I got angry.
⠀
Not with Gemma. Not even with him. With the assumption.
⠀
The assumption that because I'm 54 and divorced, that's me finished. That I should sit at the back and be grateful I was asked at all. No.
⠀
I was going to sit near the front at that wedding. And I was going to look better than anyone in that room expected.
⠀
I picked up my phone and FaceTimed my cousin Jess.
⠀
Jess runs an aesthetics clinic. She's been at it for twelve years. She's who her clients ring before weddings, reunions and the odd TV appearance.
⠀
She answered on the second ring. Took one look at me and said, "You've been crying. What's happened?"
⠀
I told her all of it. The party. Gemma. That mirror.
⠀
She went quiet for a moment. Then she said something I won't forget.
⠀
"Listen to me. Do NOT turn up to that wedding plastered in foundation and powder. If you walk in with heavy coverage creasing into every line, having spent an hour getting ready for the photos, you've proved her right. Your skin needs to actually look good. Not covered up. Sorted."
⠀
I told her I'd tried everything. Full-coverage foundations. Light ones. Primers. Setting powders. Seven shades in three years. Even the Charlotte Tilbury one every beauty editor goes on about. None of it did anything. Not really. Not for the heaviness. Not for the spots. Not for that thin, crepey texture that seemed to get worse every month.
⠀
"That's because none of those things fix what's actually wrong," she said.
⠀
She pulled something up on her screen and shared it with me. "Right. Here's what's happening to your make-up. The reason foundation starts looking heavy, patchy and crepey after about 45 has nothing to do with your technique, or your skincare, or even which brand you buy. Not really. It's something called Shade Drift."
⠀
She explained it like this:
⠀
When you're younger, your skin's thicker and more even, and it stays more or less the same colour all day. Almost every foundation ever made is built on that. You pick a shade once, it matches, and it carries on matching.
⠀
But after 45, and especially once the menopause hits and your oestrogen falls through the floor, your skin stops keeping still. It gets thinner and drier. It changes colour through the day, warmer when you're warm, greyer when you're tired. The bottle you chose at 40 can't keep up with any of that. It was never made to.
⠀
So the foundation stops matching. It sits on top instead of sinking in. Settles into every fine line. Lets the spots show through. And because it's the wrong colour on skin that's changed underneath it, it looks like a layer. A mask.
⠀
And that mask is what people see.
⠀
It's why you look shattered even with a full face on. It's why more coverage only makes it worse. You're just packing more of the wrong colour into lines that keep getting deeper.
⠀
Skin changes. The shade doesn't. It stops matching. It sits on top. It sinks into the lines. You look worn out.
⠀
That's the chain. And unless you break it right at the start, at the shade itself, nothing after that can work.
⠀
"That's why primer doesn't help," Jess said. "That's why powder doesn't help. That's why you've spent hundreds of pounds on foundations that promise the earth and do nothing. They're all the same idea: one fixed colour in a bottle. Your skin isn't one fixed colour any more. You don't need a better shade. You need a foundation that hasn't got one."
⠀
She told me about something her Korean supplier had just brought in. A colour-changing foundation from Korea, where women have been wearing this sort of thing for years.
⠀
"It's called Lambrie," she said. "And the whole clinic's obsessed with it."
⠀
She told me why.
⠀
It hasn't got a colour until it's on you. It comes out of the pump white, because the pigments are sealed in tiny capsules. As you blend it in, the warmth of your skin opens them up and your own colour comes through. Not a shade that's near enough. Yours.
⠀
Once it's matched you, it carries on moving with you. Warmer in the afternoon, cooler in the evening, the colour follows your skin rather than sitting on top of it.
⠀
And it flexes. It moves with your face rather than settling into the lines. So you're not covering anything up. You're wearing your own skin again.
⠀
The mask goes. The lines stop filling up. The crepiness smooths out.
⠀
And because the colour's genuinely yours, that tired, washed-out look goes with it. Not because anything's been "covered". Because there's no layer left for anyone to notice.
⠀
"And it's not just a foundation," Jess said. "That matters. It does the job of your primer, your concealer and your powder. Four layers of the wrong colour, gone. One pump, blend it in with your fingers, SPF 15 thrown in. Thirty seconds. That's it."
⠀
She had it sent to the hotel by the next morning.
⠀
I had five weeks between the engagement party and the wedding. Five weeks to prove Gemma wrong.
⠀
The first morning: it came out of the pump white and I thought Jess had finally lost the plot. Then I blended it in and my own colour came up under my fingers. No mask. Just my face.
⠀
That afternoon: I caught sight of myself in the car mirror at four o'clock. Nothing had moved. Nothing had crept into a single line. Normally I'd have had to redo it by lunch.
⠀
My daughter's netball match: this is where I nearly cried, and not for the usual reason. A mum I barely know came over on the sidelines and asked if I'd been away somewhere. I hadn't. I'd changed one bottle.
⠀
Week four: the spots I'd been covering for years looked softer underneath, and I'd stopped reaching for the powder. Someone at work asked if I'd done something different with my hair. I hadn't. I'd changed my foundation.
⠀
Week five. The wedding.
⠀
I was ready in ten minutes. Moisturiser. Lambrie. Mascara. Lipstick. No concealer. No primer. No powder. Nothing heavy at all.
⠀
I looked in the mirror and for the first time in over a year, I didn't wince.
⠀
My skin looked smooth. Even. Bright. Rested. Not covered up. Sorted.
⠀
The ceremony was lovely. I'll give them that.
⠀
I sat in the third row. Not at the back. Third row. The kids either side of me. My daughter squeezed my hand.
⠀
The reception was in a done-up barn. Fairy lights. Evening sun pouring in through the windows. The sort of light that shows everything.
⠀
I walked in and went straight to the bar.
⠀
That's when I felt it. That particular feeling of someone watching you.
⠀
I turned round.
⠀
My ex-husband was stood about fifteen feet away. Glass of champagne in his hand. Looking at me. Not a glance. A proper stare. The kind of look he hadn't given me in years.
⠀
Then he caught himself. Looked away. Had a sip of his drink.
⠀
But Gemma saw it.
⠀
I watched her notice from across the room. Watched her eyes go from his face to mine. Watched her jaw tighten.
⠀
Good.
⠀
Twenty minutes later, the photographer came over.
⠀
"Sorry, excuse me? I'm doing some extra portraits of guests while the light's like this. Whatever you're doing with your skin, it's catching the light beautifully. Could I get a few shots?"
⠀
I said yes.
⠀
He stood me by the window. Took six or seven. Checked the back of the camera.
⠀
"Lovely," he said. "Your skin's got this... glow to it. It's catching the light perfectly. Most women your age, sorry, that sounds awful, but most of the time I have to add a bit of light. You don't need it."
⠀
I just smiled. I didn't tell him it was a foundation that came out of the bottle white. Not yet.
⠀
There was a seating plan for dinner. I was on Table 7.
⠀
The woman next to me introduced herself as Dr Anita Kapoor. A friend of the groom's family.
⠀
We chatted for a few minutes. She was warm, straightforward, easy to talk to.
⠀
Then she stopped mid-sentence and tilted her head. "Sorry, can I ask you something personal? I'm a cosmetic dermatologist. Occupational hazard. I stare at skin."
⠀
"Go on."
⠀
"Your skin. It looks incredible. Honestly, I see results like this in my clinic and it costs thousands. Filler, laser, sometimes a mini facelift. What have you had done?"
⠀
"Nothing," I said. "It's a foundation."
⠀
She blinked. "A what?"
⠀
"A colour-changing foundation. Korean. It's called Lambrie."
⠀
I told her how it comes out white and turns into your own colour as you blend it. How it moves with your skin rather than sitting on top. How it flexes with your face so it doesn't sink into the lines.
⠀
She put her fork down. "No fixed shade at all. That's... that's actually dealing with the problem. Not just papering over it."
⠀
"Exactly."
⠀
"And that's just what you put on this morning?"
⠀
"Thirty seconds. In the hotel room."
⠀
She shook her head slowly. "My patients pay £600 to £1,200 a session for filler every six months, and the results aren't even this clean. And you've done this with a foundation, this morning." She got her phone out and started typing. "I need to look into this. My patients are going to go mad for it."
⠀
A voice behind us. "Sorry, did you just say Lambrie?"
⠀
We both turned round.
⠀
A young woman. Late twenties. Professional video camera in one hand, glass of champagne in the other.
⠀
"Sorry, I didn't mean to earwig," she said. "I'm the videographer. But I do beauty content as well. About 400K followers. I've been telling women about this colour-changing foundation for months." She was staring at my face. "Could I grab a quick clip? I'm putting together a 'wedding guest beauty' reel and your skin in this light is... honestly, it's the best skin I've seen all day. And I've been filming the bride."
⠀
I laughed. "Go on then."
⠀
She got her phone out. Filmed me in the candlelight.
⠀
Dr Kapoor was still shaking her head. "Thirty seconds. With a foundation. Unbelievable."
⠀
The videographer looked up from her screen. "My followers ask about foundation creasing and going cakey all the time. Everyone wants to know what actually fixes it. Not more concealer. Not filters. Actually fixes it. This is going to take off."
⠀
And where was Gemma while all this was going on? On the dance floor.
⠀
Her make-up artist had spent two hours on her that morning. Full-coverage foundation. Colour corrector. Setting spray. The lot.
⠀
By the first dance, her concealer was already creasing into every fine line under her eyes. By the time they cut the cake, she'd done two touch-ups. By ten o'clock, she was stood in the loos with a compact mirror doing damage control, while I was being complimented by a dermatologist and a beauty content creator at my table.
⠀
I didn't say a word to her. I didn't need to. The photographer's camera said it all.
⠀
I drove home the next morning.
⠀
For two days, I just... breathed. Felt lighter than I had in months.
⠀
Then on the third day, my phone buzzed. Instagram message. From Gemma.
⠀
"Hi. This is a bit awkward but... what foundation were you wearing at the wedding? You looked really good."
⠀
I read it three times. Then I screenshotted it. Sent it to Jess with a crying-laughing emoji and three fire emojis.
⠀
Jess rang me back within a minute, howling. "THE BRIDE IS ASKING YOU FOR MAKE-UP ADVICE?"
⠀
"The bride is asking ME for make-up advice."
⠀
We laughed till we cried.
⠀
Then Jess turned serious. "Honestly though, tell her to be quick. The 60% off might already have gone. The clinic group chat's gone mad. Everyone's trying to stock up before it goes back to full price."
⠀
I thought about it for a minute. Then I messaged Gemma back.
⠀
"It's called Lambrie. They might still have a discount on. It was ending soon when I got mine, though, so I don't know if it's still going. Good luck."
⠀
Short. Polite. Not bothered.
⠀
She left me on read.
⠀
I met Jess for dinner the week after to tell her the whole thing. She laughed so hard the next table turned round.
⠀
"See?" she said. "Clever women don't need two hours and a make-up artist. They just need the right foundation."
⠀
Then she got her phone out. "But seriously, look at this." She showed me the clinic group chat. Her colleagues were panicking, trying to get theirs before it sold out. "The last lot sold out in 48 hours. They're a small company. They make the pigments fresh in small batches, so when it's gone, it's a 4-6 week wait. If you click and it's sold out, that's that."
⠀
She looked at my face across the table. "Your timing was spot on."
⠀
I thought about Gemma. Her two-hour morning. Her make-up artist. Her concealer creasing by the first dance.
⠀
Then I looked down at the little purple bottle in my handbag.
⠀
One product. Thirty seconds in the morning. No complicated routine. No creasing. No fuss.
⠀
Here's what I know now.
⠀
For eighteen years, I was somebody's wife. When he left me for a younger woman, the assumption wasn't just that he'd traded up. It was that I'd passed my sell-by date.
⠀
Gemma actually whispered to her bridesmaid that I looked like I hadn't slept since the divorce. As if whatever I was worth had walked out the door with my husband.
⠀
So when I decided to go to that wedding anyway, I had two choices.
⠀
Turn up in heavy make-up with two hours of damage control and prove everyone right, that I was falling apart without him. Or turn up with one bottle and my own skin and prove I never needed anyone to look good.
⠀
Lambrie didn't make me beautiful. It just showed I always was.
⠀
Gemma watched the photographer take me aside for extra portraits while her own concealer was giving up. She watched her new husband stare at me across the barn. She watched the camera keep coming back to MY face.
⠀
And three days later, she messaged me asking what I was using.
⠀
The woman who felt sorry for me was asking me for help.
⠀
Some things sort themselves out.
⠀
Jess says the whole clinic is trying to get theirs before the discount page comes down. Once it's gone, Lambrie goes back to full price.
⠀
If you've ever been made to feel your best days are behind you...
⠀
If someone's ever looked at you with pity instead of respect...
⠀
If you're tired of foundation creasing into lines that get deeper every year...
⠀
You need this foundation.
⠀
Not because it's magic. Because a foundation with no fixed shade, one that moves with the skin you've got now, changes everything.
⠀
The mask isn't a coverage problem. It's a shade problem. Wear a colour that's actually yours and the mask goes, because there's no layer left to see.
⠀
The creasing isn't permanent. It's a fixed-formula problem. Wear something that flexes with your skin and it stops sinking into the lines.
⠀
The spots aren't just "age". They're what shows when the colour on top is wrong. Get the colour right, and they stop being the first thing anyone sees.
